key_findings.finding: Direct evidence specifically testing a continuous conductive paste band/bridge between adjacent standard precordial ECG electrodes V1–V6 was not identified in the PubMed searches; the evidence base is therefore mechanistic/analogous rather than a direct V1–V6 bridge experiment.

source_tools.relevance: Targeted searches for paste bridges and ECG electrode bridging returned no direct V1–V6 study; results were predominantly wearable-electrode papers.
Broader searches for electrode bridging and precordial artifact likewise did not identify a direct paste-bridge case report.

key_findings.finding: A wet conductive bridge would electrically couple neighboring skin/electrode nodes, reducing their effective impedance and partially equalizing their potentials. In a voltage-mode ECG amplifier this can cause lead cross-talk/mixing, attenuation of the true local precordial potential, and redistribution of signal between adjacent V leads; the most affected leads should be those physically connected by the paste, with effects extending to any lead whose reference/current-return path is altered. The exact amplitude and polarity are circuit- and impedance-dependent, so a fixed prediction such as uniformly increased or decreased QRS is not supported by the retrieved clinical literature.

source_tools.relevance: The retrieved ECG electrode literature establishes conductive gel as the low-impedance electrolyte at the skin-electrode interface and models signal acquisition through electrode/contact impedances.

The search identified a direct electrical-short artifact analogy in which a short circuit/impedance reduction generated abnormal recorded signals, supporting the circuit mechanism but not standard ECG morphology.

key_findings.finding: Likely waveform consequences of a paste bridge are distortion of precordial R-wave progression and QRS amplitudes, altered relative ST-T amplitudes/polarities, baseline shifts or saturation if the bridge creates a very low-impedance path, and apparent loss of normal spatial differences between adjacent V leads. Because the six precordial leads normally show a characteristic R-wave increase V1–V4 followed by decrease V4–V6, a bridge can create implausible neighboring-lead similarity or disrupted progression and should not be interpreted as true regional ischemia without repeat recording.

source_tools.relevance: The case report explicitly describes expected precordial R-wave progression and emphasizes that precordial technical artifacts can mimic pathology.

key_findings.finding: Practical guidance: prevent bridging by applying only a small, isolated amount of paste/gel under each electrode; keep inter-electrode skin dry and visibly free of continuous conductive films; avoid paste smearing during placement or sweating; inspect for gel connecting adjacent electrodes, replace contaminated electrodes, and repeat the ECG after cleaning/drying the skin and restoring correct placement. Interpret suspicious tracings by checking for abrupt or nonphysiologic changes confined to neighboring V leads, disrupted R-wave progression, identical-looking adjacent leads, baseline movement beginning before/after QRS, and discordance with symptoms, serial ECGs, limb leads, or other modalities. Do not diagnose STEMI/ischemia or QT prolongation from the contaminated tracing alone.
